$comment: Shared behavioural contract for spoken-form matching: how a name that is visible on
screen is turned into shapes a person could say, and how a heard phrase is scored
against one of those names.
This file plays the same role for SpokenForms that dictionary-test-vectors.json plays
for DictionaryCorrector, with one difference worth writing down rather than leaving to
be discovered: there is no C# implementation yet. windows/ has no SpokenForms.cs and no
runner for these cases, so today the file pins one implementation instead of holding two
in agreement. It is written as a contract anyway, because the port will be written
against it, and because a heuristic that ships before its specification never gets one.
Every number here is generated from the Swift implementation and then read by a human.
That order matters: a value that looked wrong was fixed in the code, not blessed here.
Sections, and the rule each one pins:
tokenize        - words, lowercased, punctuation dropped, digit runs whole, and UTF-16
offsets into the string that was passed in. A port that uses byte
offsets disagrees on the third case and nowhere else, which is
exactly the kind of bug that ships.
identifiers     - basename, path segments, extension and token splitting. Note that
v1.2.3 has no extension: a numeric suffix is a version, and treating
it as one would make every phrase that said 'three' look like it had
named the file's type.
phoneticKeys    - Double Metaphone, Philips' 2000 revision, truncated to 4 characters,
token by token. Downstream every score depends on these, so they are
spelled out rather than described.
phoneticMatches - which of those key pairs are allowed to meet. cache/kash must;
login/logout must not.
variants        - the spoken shapes of a name, in order, plus the single form that may
spend ASR bias budget. Order is contractual because callers truncate.
scores          - a phrase against a candidate. Each case asserts the number to within
0.0005 AND the two booleans. The number alone lets a threshold change
turn into fifty edits; the booleans alone let a port sit at 0.719
forever and still call itself green.
bestMatches     - the best window of a whole sentence, and where it landed. Indices are
into tokenize() of the transcript, filler included.
bias            - merging the user's dictionary with harvested screen names inside one
context budget. The dictionary is never reordered and never
de-duplicated; the harvest is both.
The negative cases are not filler. A false tag costs the user a word they actually said,
which is worse than a missing tag they can type themselves, so 'must not match' is as
much of the specification as 'must'.

bias.note: dictionary first, harvested appended in rank order
a harvested name the dictionary already has is dropped, whatever its case
the harvested share is a hard cap, not a proportion
a full dictionary leaves the harvest nothing, and is not reordered to make room
the limit truncates the dictionary itself rather than overflowing
no dictionary at all still spends only the harvested share
blank and whitespace-only entries are dropped, and the rest are trimmed
two dictionary rows differing only in case are both kept: they are the user's own
duplicates inside the harvest are collapsed against each other too
